Vakyartha (vak) is a local-first agent harness for one owner: agents that work on code, documents, research and everyday tasks, reached from a desktop app, the browser, a terminal and chat apps, with every model input and tool result kept in an append-only record. Its thesis is strong safety, transparent operation, extensible integrations and a simple core.

The lower layers (storage, permission, the pure deciders, the document engines) are well shaped and change rarely. Above them, three large crates (vak-core, vak-agent, vak-server) hold the turn and most features, and that is where most of the work and most of the risk sit.

Built-in tools found: agent_network, ask_parent, automations, bash, commitments, doc_read, edit, flow, forget_memory, glob, grep, mail_calendar, office_apply, plan, propose_skill, read, recall, remember, skill, task, webfetch, workers, write.

Not yet released

  • Route planning stops on unreadable evidence instead of planning from an incomplete history.
  • Budget reservations retain unresolved costs when recording fails and keep their original attribution.
  • Live outcome revisions and steering messages must be recorded before they change the running contract or reach the model.
  • Two dependency updates clear seven known vulnerabilities:
  • Concurrent credential updates preserve every presence marker, and trust checks treat unreadable presence metadata conservatively.
  • Commitment admission and portfolio reads report unreadable history instead of treating it as an empty portfolio.
  • Chart category labels retain their original text, including leading zeroes and punctuation.
  • Charts retain tiny ranges, distinguish nearby values and position extreme finite values without overflowing.
  • Tools stop before execution if their assistant message cannot be saved.
  • Saved answer and page views reopen in the Canvas after a reload.
  • Calls whose effects are unknown wait for other potentially mutating calls instead of bypassing resource conflict checks.
  • Artifact changes stop before deciding or writing when their history is unreadable.
  • Search, lists and tool-history queries refresh sharing permissions before returning results, and report unreadable sharing records instead of trusting stale grants.
  • Stopping a recovery probe no longer leaves a provider permanently unavailable.
  • Grant-service permission checks, outbound-action decisions and connected account reads now fail when new records cannot be read, rather than silently trusting cached state.
  • Ref writes and removals check the current writer epoch atomically with their commit record, so a restored store refuses a stale writer even when the two operations race.

Dependencies that point up

  • vak-catalog (L1) uses vak-llm
  • vak-config (L1) uses vak-control, vak-llm
  • vak-delivery (L2) uses vak-intent
  • vak-session (L1) uses vak-control, vak-intent, vak-llm

Each of these ties a lower layer to a higher one. When the data substrate imports model or intent types, a change to those types becomes a change to stored data, and the data contract only lets stored data grow.

The top is inverted as well. vak-core uses 25 crates, including the agent loop, so there is no small core a program could link against without pulling in nearly everything.

Sheet 06

Process topology

What runs at once on an installed machine. Drawn by hand.
long-lived processshort-lived child process, sandboxedshares fate: one process

Tools are isolated well: every built-in tool call, parser and MCP server crosses into a sandboxed child process. Everything else shares one process: the HTTP surface, the gateway, every live agent loop, provider streaming, schedulers and the storage code. The no-panic rule covers crashes, but nothing contains a slow leak, a blocking call on the async runtime, or a stuck lock. Any of those stalls every session and every channel together.

Sheet 07

One turn, end to end

Traced through the code. Drawn by hand; the names it uses are checked on every run.
  1. client → server
    The client posts a message. The server checks the bearer token, or the cookie plus a recognised Origin, then finds the live session handle and the workspace's Core in the pool.
  2. server → core
    Core::run_turn_with_message receives the session, the message, a cancel token, an approver, a permission engine, steering queues and an event channel.
  3. core
    run_turn_recorded, 1,647 lines in one function: it refuses an inactive, over-quota or standing-by Agent, takes a permission lease, resolves the route afresh, reads the capability epoch, resolves prompt layers, runs the intent resolver, picks commitments and builds the tool surface.
  4. core → ledger
    It mints the turn id and the RunId with its trace key and opens the run before anything else is written.
  5. core → agent
    The agent loop starts: run_message_inner, 1,862 lines in one function.
  6. agent → context
    plan_for_session picks the working set: the open turn word for word, plus the previous turn's card and nothing older. Assembly builds a stable prefix and a per-turn tail.
  7. llm
    complete_with_reliability walks the turn's route ladder with retries, Retry-After and the circuit breaker, and streams deltas with snapshots.
  8. agent → ledger
    Tool calls are read and normalised before the assistant message is written (read_arguments, then fill_defaults).
  9. agent
    authorize checks each call against the declared-reach permission engine and the provenance gate, and asks the approver when the answer is Ask.
  10. agent → worker
    Calls run in resource-claim waves. File and shell tools go to a sandboxed worker process. Card calls (show_card), recall, plan and task are handled inside the loop itself.
  11. worker → ledger
    Results, presentations and effects are written to the ledger. Large payloads go to the object store.
  12. agent
    Steps repeat until the model stops. Then the plan check compares the plan with receipts, and one correction goes through the ladder if something is missing.
  13. agent → ledger
    The turn card, decisions and work receipt are written, and Core settles the run.
  14. agent → server
    Agent events carry both a delta and a snapshot.
  15. server → client
    client_events::project sends what a person may see over SSE with sequence numbers, and the client draws each card by its form.

The sequence is sound and the record is thorough. Steps 3 and 5 to 12 are the two most complex functions in the system by clippy's measure, and most behaviour changes go through them; finding F1 has the evidence.

How state is kept

The substrate is a small database written by hand: encrypted content-addressed objects, per-entry sealed record frames in a hash chain, CAS refs with generations and writer epochs in SQLite, segments sealed by copy-verify-swap, Documents as versioned objects, rollups as projections, and a catalog tailer with one cursor per source.

Owning this layer, with no third-party database beyond the embedded SQLite for refs and the catalog, is a recorded decision. Its design is careful, and its size is the cost: 70 registered durable paths, each chain with its own reader, fencing on every write path, and erasure by destroying keys. The 2026-10-18 review found two P1 faults exactly in this layer:

A01: a cached grant kept authorizing after its revocation sat in an unreadable segment. A02: the global writer-epoch check and the ref update were not one transaction, so a fenced writer could still move a ref. See docs/plans/open-items.md for where their fixes stand.

One naming trap: the registry entry .env is the encrypted-file fallback for the Shared secret scope. The contract forbids literal .env files, so the name invites the wrong reading.

The work concentrates where the architecture is weakest. The three facade crates took most of the commits, while the well-shaped lower crates (permission, storage, ooxml, pdf, lifecycle) were written once and changed little.

Low churn in the lower crates is a good sign: they have clear contracts. High churn in the top three is the opposite. Every new behaviour lands in the same few files, because the boundaries that would let it land elsewhere don't exist.

Docs were touched in 57% of commits. Keeping the record true is a stated rule and it is followed, but each rule added to AGENTS.md (20,046 words) is enforced by whoever reads it, not by the type system or a crate boundary. The contract stands in for structure the code doesn't have.

Sheet 12

Critic's findings

Only findings with a cost today. Each gives its evidence, why it matters and the fix. Numbers are live; the judgements were last reviewed at 8.9.0. Method: blueprint/methods/architecture-review.md.
Structure shape of the codeVerdict what the record shows
F1
StructureCaused defects

A turn's decisions share mutable state inside two outlier functions

Evidence.

Clippy's cognitive_complexity scores Agent::run_message_inner at 194 (rank 1 of 4,348 library functions) and Core::run_turn_recorded at 103 (rank 3); the median is 3 and the 99th percentile 24. 148 commits changed the first (6% of all) and 207 the second (9%). Fix commits land in vak-core/src/lib.rs at 10.2 and vak-agent/src/lib.rs at 9.2 per thousand lines, against a median of 4.5 over 396 files; file size alone does not predict the rate (ρ = -0.14).

Why it matters.

The loop keeps the turn's decisions in mutable locals that every step and every call result updates. 948ece43d fixed two bugs of exactly that kind: receipts.unresolved_error was cleared by a later success in the same batch even when an earlier call had failed, and verification_stale came out stale or not depending on which parallel result returned first. Both were fixed by moving the decision into a pure function over the whole batch, tested on its own.

Fix.

Do that for the rest: the turn's state as one type, each decision a pure function of it, and the end-of-turn checks (among them goal mode's audit, the managed-work gate and the commitment hold, which judge durable work at different scopes on purpose) as one ordered list with tests of how they combine. Context planning and the model call can stay as they are.

Complexity table; git log -L; commit 948ece43d; evidence.py hotspots.

F2
StructureCaused a defect

The rule that wrappers forward every Tool declaration is enforced by nothing

Evidence.

The trait's width is deliberate: a tool declares what it is (34 methods, 30 with a default) so that nothing decides by a tool's name. AGENTS.md then requires that "a wrapper forwards every declaration", and no test checks it. 2 wrappers forward by hand, and one that forgets compiles cleanly and answers with the default:

  • ScopedWriteTool (crates/vak-agent/src/write_lease.rs:142): does not forward card_block, card_kinds, changes_workspace, presents_cards
  • BrokeredTool (crates/vak-tools/src/broker.rs:349): does not forward card_block, card_kinds, presents_cards

Why it matters.

fill_defaults joined the trait on 2026-10-07 (fb981ed3d), and both wrappers began forwarding it only on 2026-10-12 (53dbc16f8): for five days every brokered tool lost its argument aliases. The gaps listed above answer correctly today only because no wrapped tool overrides those methods.

Fix.

A test that fails when a wrapper leaves a defaulted method unforwarded, or a delegation macro that forwards them all.

crates/vak-tools/src/lib.rs (pub trait Tool); AGENTS.md; git log -S per method; evidence.py tool_wrappers.

F3
StructureDefects found by review

Storage's guarantees are not tested in the shapes that broke them

Evidence.

Owning the storage layer is a decision (docs/decisions.md, 2026-10-18), and it is tested for torn writes, crashes, fsync paths and injected faults, with a fuzz corpus. Nothing tests a chain's reader against a simple reference model, and few tests run two writer processes. The two P1 faults of 2026-10-18 needed exactly those shapes: a cached grant that kept authorizing because its revocation sat in an unreadable segment (A01), and a writer paused between the epoch check and the ref update (A02). A review's probes found them, not the suite.

Why it matters.

These are the guarantees authorization, erasure and sync rest on. A bug here does not show as a failed turn; it shows as access that should have ended, or a write that should have been fenced.

Fix.

A model-based test of each chain's reader against a reference, and multi-process interleavings of every fenced write path.

docs/audits/architecture-and-presentation-review-2026-10-18.md (A01, A02); crates/vak-storage, crates/vak-session.

What to keep, and a sound shape

Well-shaped parts worth keeping as they are

vak-permission1,166 lines, declared reach, universal Allow, an adversarial escape corpus. Small and central.
vak-control, vak-judge, vak-lifecyclePure deciders with no vak dependencies. The right shape for policy.
vak-context3,276 lines of pure planning and assembly over the ledger.
vak-ooxml, vak-pdfNo vak dependencies, bounded, fuzzable, run only in the worker.
The worker boundaryA versioned protocol with 14 task kinds; parsers and tools never run in the server process.
Effects, runs, cursorsAt-most-once outbound actions and unknown outcomes that are never re-sent automatically.
The provenance gatePrivate data plus someone else's words means a human approves anything that leaves the machine.
The completion judgesWhether a deliverable was produced, whether it met its requirements, a run's audited goal, a work contract and a commitment are judged separately on purpose, so produced output can never pass for proof.
vak-llm capability declarationsWire features declared by the adapter and learned from refusal, never inferred from a provider's name.
